hook.text: Your favorite white shirt has turned yellow, especially under the arms, and washing doesn't help. Don't throw it away. Seven steps bring white clothes back to bright white, without chlorine bleach, for a few dollars. Stay for step six: it's free, and it whitens.

intro.text: Clothes turn yellow because sweat, deodorant and detergent residue build up in the fibres, or because white fabric ages in storage. Washing doesn't remove that buildup. A soak does. Check the care label, test on a hidden seam, and remember the golden rule: never mix cleaning products.

youneed.text: You'll need baking soda, white vinegar, an oxygen booster powder, liquid dish soap, and a large bucket or sink. Keep chlorine bleach out of this job completely.

step-1.text: Step one. Read the care label on each item. Find out the fabric and the highest water temperature it can take. Cotton and polyester blends can usually handle hot water, while silk, wool and delicate fabrics need special care, so skip those. Separate your whites by fabric, and keep colors out of the soak. Check every piece for dyes, prints or metal buttons that might react. This simple sorting step prevents most laundry accidents. Do this before you start, and you'll avoid damage, since not every white item will handle hot water or strong soaks.

step-2.text: Step two. Lay the stained area flat, and rub in a few drops of liquid dish soap, or a paste of baking soda and a little water. Work it gently into underarm stains and collars with an old toothbrush, then let it sit for fifteen to thirty minutes. Dish soap breaks down the body oils that trap the yellow color, while the baking soda lifts discoloration. Don't use hot water directly on fresh sweat stains, since heat can set some of them. Old stains might need a second round of pretreatment, so be patient and repeat if needed.

step-3.text: Step three. Fill a basin with hot water, as hot as the care label allows. Add half a cup of baking soda, and stir until it dissolves. Add the clothes, and let them soak for one to two hours. Baking soda softens the water and lifts stains and odors. Afterward, you can rinse and add a cup of white vinegar to a fresh rinse bath, for a few minutes, which removes soap residue. Don't combine vinegar and the oxygen booster in the same soak. Keep the basin covered if there are children or pets around, and always rinse the clothes well afterward.

step-4.text: Step four. For stubborn yellowing, dissolve oxygen booster powder in hot water, following the instructions on the package. A common amount is one scoop per gallon of water. Wear gloves, because it can irritate skin. Submerge the clothes completely, and leave them to soak for four to eight hours or overnight, stirring now and then. Oxygen boosters release oxygen when dissolved in water, which breaks down stains without the harshness of chlorine bleach. Never use it on silk or wool. Never put the oxygen booster in a closed container, because it releases gas as it works. A loose lid is enough.

step-5.text: Step five. Wring out the clothes, and run them through the washing machine on the warmest cycle that the label allows. Use your regular detergent, but don't overdo it. Too much detergent leaves residue that makes whites look dull. Add half a cup of baking soda directly to the drum to boost cleaning. Wash whites only, and don't overload the machine, so the water can circulate. Before drying, check the stained area in good light. Use the sink or a bucket to rinse any soaked items first, and wring them out gently to avoid stretching the fabric.

step-6.text: Step six. Sunlight is a natural whitener. Hang your clothes outside, or lay them flat on a clean surface, in direct sun. The UV light helps fade yellow tones in cotton and linen. Avoid the dryer until you're sure the stain is gone, because heat can lock in any remaining color. If you can't dry outside, hang them near a bright window. If the yellowing is still visible, repeat the soak, as old stains sometimes need two rounds. Direct sun for a couple of hours is usually enough. Bring delicate items inside before they get too dry and stiff.

step-7.text: Step seven. Prevent yellowing in the future. Wash whites separately, and wash sweaty items promptly. Use the right amount of detergent, and add an extra rinse if you have hard water. Skip fabric softener on whites, as it can leave a film. Choose a deodorant that doesn't leave a heavy residue, and let it dry before dressing. Store clothes clean and fully dry, away from direct light and cardboard boxes, which can cause yellowing. A monthly maintenance wash with baking soda keeps whites bright and stops yellowing from taking hold.

step-8.text: If the yellow is still there, think about the cause. Sweat and body oil stains respond to soaking, but a repeat soak is often needed, so do a second round. Orange or brown spots may be rust, which needs a rust remover made for fabric, used as the label says. Test any product on a hidden seam first. Very old yellowing in aged fabric can be permanent, and more scrubbing will only wear the fibers.

step-9.text: Some white items are better left to a professional. Silk, wool, lace and anything labeled dry clean only can be ruined by a hot soak. The same goes for wedding dresses, christening gowns and family heirlooms, where a mistake cannot be undone. Tell the cleaner what the stain is and how old it is. A good cleaner can often lift a stain that has resisted home care, and will say honestly if it cannot.

step-10.text: Many yellow underarm stains form when sweat reacts with aluminum compounds in antiperspirant. A thin undershirt takes the sweat in place of your white shirt. Rinse fresh stains in cold water as soon as you can. Wash white shirts after one or two wears, because body oils build up and darken slowly. Do not overload the machine, so dirt can rinse out.

mistakes.text: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, mixing products. Never combine chlorine bleach with vinegar, ammonia or other cleaners, as it can create dangerous fumes. Second, using too much detergent, which leaves a dulling film. And third, drying the item in a hot dryer before the stain is completely gone. Heat sets stains, and then they are far harder to remove. Soak, check, and only then dry. Patience, gentle products and sunshine do most of the work.

recap.text: Let's recap. Check the labels and sort. Pretreat the yellow stains. Soak in hot water with baking soda. Try an oxygen booster soak for stubborn yellowing. Wash on a warm cycle. Dry in the sun. And keep whites white with a few simple habits. Seven steps, mostly waiting, and clothes that look new again. Do it once a month for whites that stay bright all year. Bonus sections cover what to do if the yellow stays, when to call a dry cleaner, and the habits that stop new yellowing.

outro.text: That's how you whiten yellowed white clothes without harsh bleach. If your shirts are bright again, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments which item you rescued, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow. Share this with someone whose white shirt has seen better days.

short-hook.text: White clothes turned yellow? Skip the harsh bleach and try this.

short-step-1.text: One. Rub dish soap and baking soda paste into the yellow areas.

short-step-2.text: Two. Soak in hot water with half a cup of baking soda for one to two hours.

short-step-3.text: Three. Wash, then dry in the sun. Never mix with bleach.
